p=Path('tmp/pdfs'); p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

print('METADATA',r.metadata)

 t=page.extract_text()
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n{t}')
 (p/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(t)
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The position-wise loss analysis provides a concrete empirical contribution. The three-parameter reciprocal curve reportedly achieves R² > 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints, with final-checkpoint fits around 0.98 at both model sizes. This supports a compact description of position-dependent loss in the studied settings.

The longitudinal experiments are substantial: two models trained for 400B tokens, checkpoints every 1B tokens, evaluation on Pile and PG-19, and forecasting from multiple training prefixes. Figure 1 reports substantial improvements over the selected forecasting baselines.

The paper connects its observations to an explicit forecasting procedure and concrete training interventions. Evaluating position-weighting variants on eight downstream benchmarks adds useful evidence beyond loss-curve fitting.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim lacks sufficiently independent validation. Section 3.3 selects the separation point for the best overall fit on completed training trajectories, and the functional forms are developed from these trajectories. Section 3.4 then evaluates forecasts on apparently the same runs. Restricting coefficient fitting to early checkpoints does not remove future information used in selecting the model itself. Fixing the forecasting rule before evaluating independent runs is needed; the current results do not establish the claimed prospective accuracy.

The comparisons do not establish the benefit of the position-wise decomposition. The proposed method incorporates the known cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the baselines use simpler functional forms. Once a0 and a1 are constant, Equation (10) reduces to aggregate loss = a2(N) + a constant. A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same piecewise logarithmic/cosine construction is therefore an essential control. Without it, the gains may primarily reflect schedule information rather than the proposed token-level analysis.

The conclusions about position weighting exceed the evidence. Equal loss-decrease rates under uniform weighting do not imply that alternative weighting cannot improve training. Table 2 examines only three suppression strategies introduced after 100B tokens, and reports no uncertainty or repeated-seed results. Similar average benchmark scores support a limited robustness observation, not statistical equivalence or the general conclusion that position weighting is unnecessary. Whether weighted losses are renormalized also needs clarification.

The claimed scope and novelty need narrowing. Evidence comes from two sizes within one architecture family, one training corpus, one training budget, and one scheduler; PG-19 changes the evaluation distribution, not the training conditions. Applications to hyperparameter selection, data-mixture selection, and early stopping are proposed but not demonstrated. Moreover, Kaplan et al. already examine loss as a function of training steps, so the claim that temporal training behavior was previously untouched is inaccurate.

Reproducibility is insufficiently documented. The promised appendix of fitted parameters is absent from the supplied manuscript. The fitting algorithm, initialization and constraints, batch size needed to convert warmup steps into tokens, and evaluation implementation are not adequately specified; no fitting code or loss trajectories are linked. The separation point is also inconsistent: 2/5 of the stated 400B-token budget is 160B, whereas Section 4.1 states 120B. These details affect the central forecasting procedure and require resolution before a sound Findings recommendation.

Equation (5) is not a generally valid probability inequality: additional context does not guarantee that the next realized word receives higher probability than a different preceding word. A conditional-entropy argument would require an expectation and appropriate distributional assumptions. This does not invalidate the observed reciprocal fits, but their motivation should be presented as an empirical hypothesis rather than a general probabilistic principle.
